transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-10-08 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~62 mins | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Samir (SE), Elena (SE), Brian (Acme Head ML Infra), Nora (Security), Kevin (Platform)

00:00 Speaker 1 (Maya): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you carving out the time. Quick roll call?
00:07 Speaker 2 (Brian): Brian here.
00:08 Speaker 3 (Nora): Nora on security.
:09 Speaker 4 (Kevin): Kevin, infra.
00:12 Speaker 1 (Maya): Great, Samir and Elena from our side will drive the deep dive. Goal: walk through tradeoffs between Hosted and Dedicated for your workload, dig into latency profiles, KV caching and batching behavior, and surface the operational differences for a VPC/on-prem pilot.

02:05 Speaker 2 (Brian): To set context: we run real-time route optimization for last-mile deliveries. Typical requests are short prompts ~40 tokens but with bursts up to 300 QPS per region. Latency SLO is p95 < 120ms for inference response. Cost is a major driver, and we also have strict data residency and audit requirements.
02:30 Speaker 5 (Samir): Thanks. Quick clarifying q: are those 300 QPS sustained or spiky bursts?
02:36 Speaker 2 (Brian): Spiky — we see peaks during dispatch windows, maybe 2-3x baseline for 2-5 minutes.
03:01 Speaker 5 (Samir): Good — that informs batching and autoscale choices. Ok, Elena, we'll hand over to you for runtime specifics.

03:15 Speaker 4 (Elena): Cool. First, high level: Hosted mode gives you immediate scale and our multi-tenant routing; Dedicated gives isolated GPU pools with predictable throughput and no noisy neighbor. For p95 latency targets you can reach them on both, but the operational levers differ.
03:40 Speaker 3 (Nora): We care about isolation: does Dedicated guarantee no cross-tenant data leakage, and how about performance isolation?
03:50 Speaker 4 (Elena): Dedicated is tenant-isolated at the runtime layer — separate GPU pools, dedicated VMs or instances. No cross-tenant model KV cache sharing. Performance isolation: since capacity is reserved, noisy neighbors from other customers don't affect you. Hosted is multi-tenant; we do smart routing and tenant-aware scheduling but during extreme cluster-wide contention you can see latency tail increases.

06:10 Speaker 5 (Samir): Let's jump into KV cache — for repeated prefix requests KV cache is the biggest win for latency. For your 40-token common prefixes, we see typical per-token reductions of 30-60% on p95 when prefix cache hits are high. Important note: in Hosted we use a distributed KV cache sharded across nodes; in Dedicated the cache is colocated within your pool and we can size it deterministically.
06:50 Speaker 2 (Brian): If we go Dedicated, how do cache invalidation and warm-up look during rollouts?
07:05 Speaker 5 (Samir): Good q. On Dedicated you control model rollout windows; we support rolling restarts with gradual traffic shift. Cache invalidation happens at model-change boundaries; the runtime keeps the KV until an explicit model version change triggers eviction. Warm-up: we recommend a small staged traffic ramp or synthetic warmers — the KV warm-up typically takes a few seconds to a few minutes depending on working set.

09:15 Speaker 4 (Elena): For Hosted, we do opportunistic warm-up and cross-customer pre-warming heuristics, but it's less deterministic. If your workload is highly sensitive to cold start tails, Dedicated gives tighter control.

11:00 Speaker 2 (Brian): Batching — our team is worried about latency vs throughput. What batching strategies do you recommend?
11:15 Speaker 5 (Samir): We use dynamic continuous batching. For low-latency you can set max batching delay to ~5ms to preserve p95, but you'll sacrifice batching efficiency. For cost optimization, allow 20-30ms max delay and enable workload-aware batch sizing. With your short prompts and bursts, a hybrid policy: small immediate batches for 90% of traffic and opportunistic large batches during spikes is a good fit.
11:50 Speaker 4 (Elena): On Dedicated, since throughput is predictable, we can tune batching aggressively and still hit latency SLOs; on Hosted, batching is subject to overall cluster load and may vary.

14:40 Speaker 3 (Nora): Quantization: we have concerns about quality regressions. Does Redwood support 8-bit and 4-bit? What quality delta do you typically see?
14:55 Speaker 5 (Samir): We do. Our supported quant profiles include 8-bit and Q4 variants. For many open models, 8-bit shows negligible quality delta on classification/short-generation tasks; Q4 may show minor token-level regressions on very fine-grained tasks. We recommend running your evaluation prompt set — we can run an automated eval with your prompts and report BLEU/ROUGE/EM or custom metrics.
15:30 Speaker 2 (Brian): Could quantization change KV cache effectiveness?
15:40 Speaker 5 (Samir): Not directly. Quantization affects model compute speed and memory, which can change throughput and therefore batching behavior; cache hit semantics remain the same. However, latency improvements from quant may reduce the need for large batching.

18:10 Speaker 4 (Elena): Noisy neighbor scenarios — Hosted has mitigation: smart routing, soft capacity reservations for high-tier customers, and preemptible fallbacks. But in sustained cluster saturation, p95 tails can move. Dedicated avoids that because you reserve nodes and GPUs for your workloads. If you want SLA-backed latency guarantees, Dedicated + reserved burst capacity is the recommended path.
18:50 Speaker 2 (Brian): Are there formal throughput SLAs for Dedicated?
19:00 Speaker 4 (Elena): Yes — contractual throughput guarantees are available on Dedicated contracts. We size the GPU pool and set expected tokens/sec targets; in the rare event of hardware failures we have failover policies and optional hot standby. The SLA language is in the contract addendum — we'll share a sample.

21:20 Speaker 3 (Nora): On the security front, for VPC/on-prem we need KMS/HSM integration, audit logs, SSO, and data retention controls. How is that handled?
21:35 Speaker 1 (Maya): For Private deployments or Dedicated within your VPC, we integrate with customer KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, HashiCorp Vault) and can support HSM-backed keys. Audit logs are shipped to your logging endpoint; SSO/SAML and SCIM for user provisioning are standard. We'll surface the security playbook PDF after this call.

23:10 Speaker 4 (Elena): Network constraints on on-prem: model weights are large — pulling models initially can take time. We support pre-loading weights into air-gapped clusters via our on-prem tooling. Also, KV cache in on-prem is local to the pool; network latency to model storage matters for restarts.

25:40 Speaker 2 (Brian): Regarding cost: do you have guidance on when Dedicated becomes more cost-effective vs Hosted?
25:55 Speaker 5 (Samir): Generally, when you have steady sustained throughput and need isolation, Dedicated makes sense. If your bursts are large but short and you don't need strict SLAs, Hosted can be cheaper because you only pay for consumed tokens/throughput. We'll produce a cost model showing break-even points given your QPS profile.

28:30 Speaker 4 (Elena): Also consider operational overhead. Dedicated shifts more responsibility to capacity planning but reduces unexpected tail spikes from multi-tenancy. Private on-prem adds more ops work (networking, KMS, storage).

30:00 Speaker 6 (Kevin): A couple of infra-specifics: our cluster uses a mix of A100 and H100 equivalent nodes; we also have 100Gb interconnect within region but VPC peering to Redwood would add ~5-10ms. How does that affect latency?
30:20 Speaker 5 (Samir): Interconnect latency is additive. If your application calls across peering with 5-10ms add, that consumes budget. For p95 <120ms you need to budget network + model inference + queuing. With H100 we see per-token lower compute latency. We can model your end-to-end budget given your network numbers.

33:10 Speaker 2 (Brian): For the bursts, can we configure burst pools that sit idle but can be used quickly?
33:25 Speaker 4 (Elena): Yes — Dedicated supports burst capacity policies: reserved standby nodes that spin up in < 90s or warm standby with warmed models that can be hot-swapped in < 10s depending on setup. There's a cost tradeoff for keeping nodes warm.

35:00 Speaker 3 (Nora): Auditability: do you log prompt contents by default? We have rules about sensitive PII — we'd prefer redaction or not logging prompts.
35:15 Speaker 1 (Maya): You control logging. For sensitive workloads we support disabling request payload logging, or we can configure on-the-fly redaction and tokenization before logs reach our systems. For Dedicated/Private you can route logs to your own S3/logging endpoint so Redwood doesn't retain raw prompts.

37:40 Speaker 5 (Samir): Quick demo snippet — (Samir shares screen) showing perf dashboard: token-level latency distribution, cache hit rate, batching windows, and model-level throughput. Example: with KV cache hit rate at 70% p95 dropped from 160ms to 85ms in demos.
38:30 Speaker 2 (Brian): That's promising. Can you re-run the demo with our representative prompt set?
38:40 Speaker 5 (Samir): Absolutely — we'll run a bench with your prompt set and give both Hosted and Dedicated profiles. We'll include quantized runs too. Expect results in the spreadsheet.

41:00 Speaker 4 (Elena): A note on model variants and fallbacks: Hosted can do automatic fallback to smaller variants during saturation; Dedicated is pinned but you can configure automatic spillover to Hosted if you want hybrid reliability. Some customers run hybrid: Dedicated primary + Hosted overflow.
41:35 Speaker 2 (Brian): Hybrid sounds interesting — what's the complexity?
41:45 Speaker 5 (Samir): Routing policies are policy-as-config — you can define percent cutovers, latency thresholds, or capacity-based fallbacks. We also support sticky sessions for stateful chat-like workloads; for stateless inference it's simpler.

44:10 Speaker 6 (Kevin): For on-prem, what's the recommended GPU per model? Our team wants guidance for provisioning so we can trial internally.
44:25 Speaker 4 (Elena): We'll share a sizing table mapping model family + sequence length + target QPS to GPU counts. E.g., for a 7B model at 40-token sequences and 300 sustained QPS you'll need X GPUs with continuous batching; we'll compute that precisely in the sizing doc.

46:30 Speaker 3 (Nora): Any gotchas around quantized model debugging? If we see hallucination increases, what's the rollback process?
46:45 Speaker 5 (Samir): Rollbacks are model-versioned. We recommend canary traffic to a small percentage, run automatic evals, and if drift is detected we roll back the quantized variant. The KV cache is keyed to model version, so rollback restores previous cache behavior.

49:20 Speaker 2 (Brian): On the legal side, what does the contract look like for Dedicated? Minimum commit periods?
49:35 Speaker 1 (Maya): Typically 6-12 month commits for Dedicated capacity with tiered discounts. We'll share a contract template and the SLA addendum.

51:00 Speaker 4 (Elena): Operational playbook: we'll provide runbooks for warmers, model rollouts, incident troubleshooting (CPU/GPU metrics, KV cache miss hot paths).

53:10 Speaker 6 (Kevin): Quick question about observability: do logs include token-level latency traces?
53:20 Speaker 5 (Samir): Yes — per-request token timing, batch composition, and cache hit/miss tags. We stream those to your trace collector or Redwood Console.

56:05 Speaker 3 (Nora): For the on-prem pilot, network and KMS are blockers; we'll need an architecture review with our security team before Oct 20.
56:20 Speaker 1 (Maya): We'll schedule that; action item noted.

58:00 Speaker 2 (Brian): Recap — you will send perf spreadsheet and config recommendations, sizing and cost model for Dedicated, and a security playbook. We'll share cluster details and a sample prompt set.
58:20 Speaker 5 (Samir): Correct. Also we'll include recommended batching settings (showing max batching delay tradeoffs), quantization runs, and hybrid routing examples.

60:00 Speaker 1 (Maya): Any final questions?
60:04 Speaker 2 (Brian): Not for now, thanks.
60:10 Speaker 3 (Nora): Thanks everyone.
60:15 Speaker 4 (Elena): Thanks — we'll follow up with materials.
60:30 Meeting ends.

Notes: transcript contains typical transcription imperfections — some speaker labels generic. Shared artifacts: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/acme_oct2026_demo (link placeholder), Security Playbook PDF (drive link to be shared).
